title: After Losing TPS, Some Haitians Flee to Canada Rather Than Face Deportation
excerpt: With Temporary Protected Status for more than 330,000 Haitians ended by the Supreme Court and the Trump administration urging them to leave, a growing number are heading north to Quebec — but the crossing carries its own dangers.
body:
• More than 330,000 Haitians lost their Temporary Protected Status on August 5 after a 6-3 Supreme Court ruling allowed the Trump administration to strip their protections.
  • A growing number of Haitians are heading to Canada, particularly French-speaking Quebec, according to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and migrant rights advocates.
  • Under a 2023 U.S.-Canada agreement, migrants caught illegally crossing the border are immediately returned to U.S. custody and can face deportation. Those who evade capture for two weeks can apply for asylum.
  • Haitians with TPS contributed approximately $4.4 billion annually to the U.S. economy, and about 2,000 TPS holders in Massachusetts alone worked in nursing homes.

A Status That Was Never Meant to Be Permanent

For 16 years, Haitians in the United States lived under a legal arrangement that was always temporary by design but functioned, in practice, as something close to permanent. Temporary Protected Status, first granted after the devastating 2010 earthquake, was renewed successively through the Obama, Trump, and Biden administrations as conditions in Haiti — gang violence, political collapse, humanitarian crisis — never improved enough to justify sending people back.

https://x.com/USATODAY/status/2088626851757404338

That arrangement ended on August 5 when TPS protections expired following a 6-3 Supreme Court ruling in June that allowed the Trump administration to terminate the designation. Justice Samuel Alito wrote for the majority that courts have limited power to review executive decisions about TPS, rejecting arguments that the administration was motivated by racial prejudice.

"The T in TPS stands for TEMPORARY," James Percival, general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, wrote on X after the ruling.

Heading North

Now, with work authorization gone and the administration urging them to leave — offering a $2,600 payment and a free flight home — some Haitians are looking to Canada instead, according to USA Today.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police confirmed an increasing number of Haitians seeking refuge in Canada, particularly in French-speaking Quebec. French is one of Haiti's official languages, making the province a natural draw. The number of Haitians seeking protection in Canada from all countries sharply rose from 7,864 in 2024 to 14,192 in 2025, according to the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada.

"As policies change, as people are stripped of their status, as this chaos unfolds, if people no longer feel safe in the United States, of course they're going to come to Canada."

— Julia Sande, Amnesty International

A Dangerous Crossing

But the route north is fraught with risk. Under a March 2023 U.S.-Canada agreement, most migrants caught illegally crossing the border are immediately taken into custody by U.S. immigration authorities and can face deportation. Those who evade capture may later qualify for refugee status.

A loophole in Canadian law allows refugees who cross undetected and remain for two weeks to apply for asylum. This has spawned a smuggling network in which asylum-seekers pay roughly $1,000 each for GPS coordinates and instructions on evading surveillance cameras, waiting out the 14-day period in Montreal-area safe houses, according to the RCMP.

"The stakes are so high at the border and a lot of people are not very well informed," said Jenn McIntyre of the Canada-U.S. Border Rights Clinic. "The consequences are profound."

The Cost of Removal

The human and economic toll of ending TPS extends well beyond the individuals affected. Haitians with TPS work authorization contributed about $4.4 billion annually to the U.S. economy through payroll and other taxes, according to the Public Rights Project. Many had lived in the United States for over a decade, owning homes and businesses, starting families, and raising U.S.-citizen children.

In Massachusetts alone, approximately 45,000 Haitians lost TPS, with 2,000 of them working in nursing homes, said Sarang Sekhavat of the Massachusetts Immigrant and Refugee Advocacy Coalition. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican, warned that removing diligent workers would hurt the state economy and leave the healthcare industry short-staffed.

In Springfield, Ohio — where Trump and Vice President JD Vance claimed without evidence during the 2024 campaign that Haitians were eating pets — some Haitians have been fitted with GPS-based ankle monitors limiting their movement to within 75 miles of home.

No Good Options

The U.S. government itself warns Americans not to travel to Haiti, citing widespread violence, crime, and kidnapping. The country lacks an effective central government, and criminal gangs control much of the capital. More than 1.4 million Haitians have been displaced by violence internally, according to the International Organization for Migration.

"A lot of folks — it's very difficult to just pick up and leave," Sekhavat said. "The idea of going back to Haiti, for the majority of folks, is just not really an option at all."
nri_angle: The termination of TPS raises questions about the security of temporary immigration protections broadly, with implications for other immigrant communities in the United States. The ruling also opens a path for ending TPS for nationals of other countries including Nepal and Venezuela.
author: Diaspora Desk
